# Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) — The HESED Reader's Guide
**Guide by:** HESED (חֶסֶד — Lovingkindness)

---

## At a Glance
| | |
|---|---|
| **Author** | Jesus ben Eleazar ben Sira, Jerusalem sage and scribe |
| **Date** | c. 180 BCE (Hebrew original); c. 132 BCE (Greek translation by grandson) |
| **Audience** | Young Jewish men entering public life; students of the wisdom tradition |
| **Genre** | Wisdom literature — instruction, maxims, hymns, praise poetry, theological reflection |
| **Timeline** | Written before the Maccabean crisis, in the last generation of "normal" Second Temple Judaism |
| **In One Sentence** | The last great sage of Israel gathers everything he has learned about God, creation, Torah, and human life — and hands it to the next generation before the world changes forever. |

---

## The World Behind the Text

Ben Sira wrote in a Jerusalem that was, for the moment, at peace. The Ptolemies of Egypt had governed Judea for over a century, and Hellenistic culture had been flowing into Jewish life steadily — Greek language, Greek philosophy, Greek manners, Greek ideas about education and the ideal person. It was a moment of intellectual ferment rather than crisis. The great question was not yet "will you die for the Torah?" but rather "how does the Torah relate to all this Greek wisdom? Can a Jewish sage hold Proverbs and Homer in the same mind? What does it mean to be educated now?"

Ben Sira answered this question from a position of supreme confidence. He was a man of the city — a Jerusalem intellectual who had traveled, who had sat in courts and deliberated with rulers, who had studied the full range of what we might call the liberal arts, ancient style. His school, the beth midrash (house of study, mentioned in 51:23), was a real institution where real students came to learn. He taught rhetoric, history, natural philosophy, ethics, and above all, the literature of Israel. He was deeply conversant with every part of what would become the Hebrew Bible — Proverbs, Psalms, the Prophets, the Torah, the historical books. He quotes and alludes to all of them.

What makes Ben Sira remarkable is his identification of Wisdom with Torah. In Proverbs 8, Wisdom is a divine feminine figure who existed before creation, who was with God when the world was made. She is cosmic, mysterious, universal. Ben Sira accepts this portrait entirely — and then, in chapter 24, makes a move that no previous text had made explicitly: Wisdom, he says, searched all creation for a dwelling place and was commanded by God to "make your dwelling in Jacob, and in Israel receive your inheritance." She pitched her tent among the people of God, and that tent is the Torah: "All this is the book of the covenant of the Most High God, the law that Moses commanded us" (24:23). Wisdom is not abstract or universal; she is the Torah of Israel. To pursue wisdom is to study Torah, and to study Torah is to find the ordering principle of the cosmos.

---

## Why This Book Was Written

The Prologue, written by Ben Sira's grandson when he translated the book into Greek (c. 132 BCE), is one of the most valuable documents in the deuterocanonical literature. The grandson explains that his grandfather, "after devoting himself especially to the reading of the Law and the Prophets and the other books of our ancestors, and after acquiring considerable proficiency in them, was himself also led to write something pertaining to instruction and wisdom, so that by becoming familiar also with his book those who love learning might make even greater progress in living according to the law."

Ben Sira wrote to equip young Jewish men — particularly those headed for careers in public service, the courts, the diplomatic corps, the temple administration — for lives of integrity and excellence. Much of the book reads like a curriculum: how to speak in public (4:23–25, 20:5–8), how to behave at a dinner party (31:12–32:13), how to choose friends (6:5–17), how to treat servants (7:20–21), how to relate to women (26:1–4), how to handle money (29:1–7), how to think about death (38:16–23), how to seek medical care (38:1–15). This is practical wisdom for real life, rooted in the conviction that the Torah is not merely ceremonial law but a comprehensive instruction in how to be human.

The book also carries a polemic edge, though it is subtle. Ben Sira is writing in the presence of Hellenistic wisdom traditions — Stoicism, Epicureanism, the various philosophical schools that were the intellectual prestige culture of his day. He engages them implicitly, appropriating their categories while insisting that Israel's tradition is deeper and truer. The famous passage beginning "Let us now praise famous men" (44:1ff.) — the Praise of the Ancestors — is partly a response to Greek lists of heroes and benefactors of humanity. Israel has its own heroes, Ben Sira says. They are better.

---

## How to Read This Book

Sirach resists the kind of linear reading that narrative books invite. It is an anthology — poems, maxims, extended meditations, hymns, prayers — loosely organized but not always in a clear sequence. The best approach is thematic rather than strictly sequential, at least for a first reading.

Several extended passages reward sustained attention. Chapter 1 opens with a meditation on Wisdom that frames the entire book: "All wisdom is from the Lord, and with him it remains forever" (1:1). Chapter 24 is the theological heart — Wisdom's self-praise, her identification with Torah, and the river imagery that grounds divine wisdom in the created world. Read these together as a diptych.

Chapters 44–50, the "Praise of the Ancestors," are among the most beautiful extended passages in the deuterocanonical literature. Ben Sira moves through Israel's entire history — Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Aaron, Phinehas, Joshua, Caleb, the Judges, Samuel, Nathan, David, Solomon, Elijah, Elisha, Hezekiah, Isaiah, Josiah, Ezra, Nehemiah, Zerubbabel — with a poet's compression and a theologian's eye for what each figure contributes to the covenant story. The passage culminates in chapter 50 with a dazzling description of Simon the High Priest — a living person at the time of Ben Sira's writing — conducting the Temple service. It reads almost cinematically: the procession, the vestments, the incense smoke, the trumpet blast, the people prostrate in awe. This is the world Ben Sira inhabits and loves, and he wants his readers to love it with him.

Chapter 38:1–15, "Honor the Physician," is worth reading as an independent unit. It is the ancient world's most sophisticated statement about the relationship between divine healing and medical science — they are not in competition; the physician's skill is itself a gift of God. The passage was quoted repeatedly in the medieval debates about whether seeking medical care showed insufficient faith. Ben Sira's answer, nearly 2,200 years ago, was: pray and take your medicine.

---

## The Threads — How This Book Connects

Sirach is the most densely intertextual book in the deuterocanon. Ben Sira had clearly memorized the full range of Israelite literature, and his book is a sustained meditation on it. His debt to Proverbs is most obvious — the genre, the style, the topics, the opening identification of Wisdom with the fear of the Lord (1:14 echoes Proverbs 1:7 and 9:10). But he also engages deeply with Job (especially on the problem of suffering and the inscrutability of divine ways), with Psalms (his own hymn in chapter 39 and thanksgiving in chapter 51 are clearly modeled on the Psalter), and with the wisdom of the great sages.

The Wisdom identification with Torah in chapter 24 has a direct literary heir in John 1:1–14. John's prologue — "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God... and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us" — is in direct conversation with Sirach 24 (and Proverbs 8). The Greek word for "dwelt" in John 1:14 (eskenosen, "pitched his tent") echoes Wisdom pitching her tent in Israel (Sirach 24:8). Christian theology about Christ as the incarnation of divine Wisdom drew explicitly on this tradition.

The Praise of the Ancestors (44–50) prefigures the famous "Hall of Faith" in Hebrews 11, which similarly surveys Israel's ancestors as exemplars of trust in God. The genres are different — Ben Sira's heroes are honored for wisdom and covenant faithfulness, Hebrews' for faith — but the impulse is identical: to show that the present community stands in a long line of those who have trusted and been vindicated.

Ben Sira's statement on free will — "Do not say, 'It was the Lord's doing that I fell away'... He has not commanded anyone to be wicked, and he has not given anyone permission to sin" (15:11–20) — anticipates debates about determinism and freedom that would occupy Jewish and Christian theology for centuries. His position is as clear as anything in the tradition: God gives choices; humans are responsible for them.

---

## What a Modern Reader Might Miss

The Hebrew original matters more than most readers realize. For most of Christian history, Sirach was known only in its Greek translation, and that translation, though generally excellent, introduces subtle shifts in emphasis. Beginning in 1896, fragments of the Hebrew original began surfacing — first from the Cairo Genizah (a storage room in a synagogue where worn manuscripts were deposited), then from Masada, then from Qumran. Today, approximately two-thirds of the Hebrew text has been recovered. In several places, the Hebrew and Greek diverge significantly, and the Hebrew shows a more direct, less polished voice that connects more immediately to Proverbs and the rest of the Hebrew wisdom tradition.

The passage on women in Sirach (25:13–26, 26:1–18, 42:9–14) is jarring to modern readers, and fairly so. Ben Sira's misogynistic passages — "A man's wickedness is better than a woman's goodness" (42:14 in some versions) — represent one side of the ancient Jewish wisdom tradition's ambivalence about women, an ambivalence already present in Proverbs (the "strange woman" of Proverbs 7 alongside the "capable wife" of Proverbs 31). The passages do not erase the book's value, but they should not be smoothed over. They reflect a patriarchal society in which women's honor was the primary mechanism of family reputation, and they reveal the anxieties that structure created.

The author's social world is elite. Ben Sira writes from the perspective of an educated Jerusalem man with access to courts, symposia, and travel. The book's wisdom is oriented toward navigating public life in positions of influence. The poor appear largely as objects of charity rather than as wisdom teachers in their own right. This is different from the prophetic tradition (which frequently positions the poor as the ones through whom God speaks) and even from parts of the Psalter. Ben Sira's is a wisdom of the educated center, and it should be read as such.

---

## Why This Book Isn't in Your Bible

Sirach's canonical history is unusually well-documented. Jerome, translating the Vulgate in the late fourth century, knew it was not in the Hebrew canon but included it in his Latin Bible under the name Ecclesiasticus ("the church's book") — a title that reflects its widespread liturgical use in the early church for catechesis and moral instruction. The title itself is a canonical argument: this is the book the church uses for teaching.

The Hebrew canon excluded it, probably because it was written too recently (c. 180 BCE) to qualify as ancient Scripture, and because its author was known — a named, historical figure rather than a legendary ancient sage. The rabbinic tradition, which established canonical limits partly to exclude sectarian writings, also had reasons to be cautious about a book so clearly connected to the Second Temple priestly establishment. Yet Sirach was never entirely excluded from Jewish use: it continued to be quoted by rabbis in the Talmud (sometimes with the formula used to introduce Scripture), and the preservation of its Hebrew in the Cairo Genizah shows that Jewish communities were copying it in Hebrew as late as the medieval period.

For Christians, the book's canonical status was debated but its liturgical use was universal. Augustine and the Council of Hippo (393 CE) included it in the canon; Protestant reformers excluded it following Jerome's own ambivalence about books not in the Hebrew canon; the Council of Trent defined it as canonical for Catholics. The Eastern Orthodox churches include it; the Anglican tradition places it in the Apocrypha with a recommendation for edification rather than doctrine. It remains, in many ways, the most "used" of the deuterocanonical books — quoted in liturgy, relied on for moral instruction, and surprisingly current in its observations about human nature.

---

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| c. 220–215 BCE | Ben Sira likely born; educated in Jerusalem |
| c. 196 BCE | Simon II (the High Priest praised in ch 50) dies; Ben Sira likely witnessed his ministry |
| c. 180 BCE | Ben Sira writes the book in Hebrew |
| 175 BCE | Antiochus IV takes power; world Ben Sira knew begins to unravel |
| 167–164 BCE | Maccabean revolt — Ben Sira either died before this or in its early stages |
| c. 132 BCE | Grandson arrives in Egypt and begins Greek translation |
| c. 132–117 BCE | Grandson completes the Greek translation; writes the Prologue |
| 1896 CE | Solomon Schechter discovers Hebrew fragments in Cairo Genizah |
| 1964 CE | Hebrew fragments found at Masada by Yigael Yadin |

---
